result: Artificial selection for blue wing color in J. coenia resulted in a 74% increase in lamina thickness in cover scales (from 107±14 nm in wild-type brown to 187±18 nm in selected blue), causing a color shift from brown to blue.
evaluation: All three reviewers praised the artificial selection experiment and found the lamina thickness measurements convincing. Reviewer 1 stated the work 'provides an in-depth look at structural color production' using 'directional selection,' and Reviewer 3 noted the study was 'methodologically correct' with measurements that 'faithfully follow the underlying physical principle.' The only concern raised was about pseudo-replication in statistics (Reviewer 2), which is a methodological issue rather than a challenge to the core finding.

result: Deletion of the optix gene via CRISPR knockout increased lamina thickness (to 212±11 nm) and reduced pigmentation in cover scales, producing blue coloration through mechanisms similar to artificial selection.
evaluation: Reviewers were enthusiastic about the optix findings. Reviewer 1 noted 'they find that a single gene, optix, can control both the production of pigment and structural color (via modification of lamellar thickness)' and called this 'interesting.' Reviewer 2 appreciated 'the emphasis on the interaction between structural and pigment colours.' The acceptance summary highlighted that 'the authors' identification of optix as a gene that controls both the production of pigment and structural color is of great interest.'

result: The optix gene exhibits context-specific regulation, controlling both pigmentation and lamina thickness simultaneously across different wing regions and scale types, making it a candidate pathway for coordinated color evolution.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly praised this finding: 'The finding that optix is so highly context dependent is interesting. It provides a hint at underlying developmental mechanism.' The reviewer noted this suggests 'scale-building cells still rely on combinatorial inputs from positional information.' The acceptance summary emphasized this should be 'further explored in future studies,' indicating acceptance of the finding while recognizing more work is needed.

result: Blue and brown geographic variants of J. evarete differ in lamina thickness (199±14 nm vs 112±13 nm), with non-overlapping distributions, and artificially selected J. coenia recapitulates this natural variation.
evaluation: Reviewers accepted the comparative data across species. Reviewer 2 noted 'There is an impressive body of comparative data from across the genus' and Reviewer 3 stated the study was 'conducted on a very broad and sensible selection of specimens from the different taxa.' The recapitulation of natural variation through artificial selection was implicitly accepted as part of the overall positive assessment of the selection experiment.

result: Lamina thickness varies continuously across Junonia species (90-260 nm range) and has a consistent relationship with structural color wavelength, following Newton's series, suggesting recurrent evolution via lamina thickness adjustments at both micro- and macroevolutionary scales.
evaluation: While reviewers praised the comparative data (Reviewer 2: 'impressive body of comparative data'), Reviewer 2 raised confusion about the relationship between thickness and color: 'greater thickness is associated with a shift from brown to blue, but it is stated that function shifts towards longer wavelengths as thickness increases' which 'seems in the wrong direction.' This indicates the reviewers found the presentation of this relationship unclear, though they did not reject the underlying data.

result: Wing color in Junonia is determined by complex interactions between lamina structural color and pigmentation, with lamina structural colors contributing significantly to color diversity beyond what pigmentation alone can explain.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 specifically 'appreciated the emphasis on the interaction between structural and pigment colours which is not emphasised often enough,' indicating strong support for this aspect of the work. Reviewer 3 noted the study shows how 'variations in scale lamina thickness lead to the creation of colorful reflections' and praised the comprehensive approach.

result: Thin film optical modeling qualitatively describes the reflectance data, though modeled curves are systematically blue-shifted by 40-80 nm relative to observed spectra. Modeling also reveals likely UV reflectance from laminae.
evaluation: Reviewer 2 noted confusion about this section: 'I was unsure which is Supplementary Figure 3A which is the only result presented in this section (the only supplement to Figure 3 is a table),' indicating presentation problems. Reviewer 3 raised concerns about the systematic deviation and asked whether metallic coating or vacuum dehydration could contribute to the 40-80 nm offset. Reviewer 3 also emphasized that UV reflectance data were missing from measurements (only from models), calling this 'a great pity' and noting UV is 'biologically relevant.'

result: Because laminae are intrinsic components of typical butterfly scales and thin films occur broadly across Lepidoptera, tuning lamina thickness represents an available and likely conserved mechanism for creating structural color across the order.
evaluation: This broader implication was accepted by reviewers as part of the overall positive assessment. Reviewer 3 noted the study 'largely builds on the existing work' but represents 'an incremental advance demonstrated on a very nicely chosen set of taxa, all presented in a very convincing and comprehensive way.' The reviewers' enthusiasm for the system's tractability implicitly supports these broader conclusions.

result: The possibility that optix plays a role in patterning blue wing regions in artificially selected J. coenia is intriguing and motivates investigation of whether optix was a target of selection.
evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly requested more direct evidence: 'it would be fantastic to directly connect the gene that potentially controls structural color (optix) with the evolutionary changes observed' through expression analysis or genetic crosses. The reviewer stated 'Any number of downstream genes might also influence lamina thickness' and that while optix is 'likely' responsible, 'this should be demonstrated/tested more directly.' The editors noted this would take too long for revision and asked authors to 'simply discuss this issue in the paper.'

result: Blue scales contain brown pigment in ridges but the bare lamina is sufficient for blue structural color. Artificial selection increased pigmentation in ground scales, enhancing color saturation without removing pigment from cover scales.
evaluation: This detailed mechanistic work was implicitly accepted as part of the reviewers' overall positive assessment of the artificial selection experiment. Reviewer 2's appreciation for 'the emphasis on the interaction between structural and pigment colours' encompasses these findings about pigment distribution and its effects.

result: In optix mutants, ground scales had thick laminae (199±31 nm) and increased pigmentation, while different wing regions showed varied effects including melanin production in ventral regions and conversion of orange discal bars to blue through both lamina thickening and pigment changes.
evaluation: These detailed phenotypic observations in optix mutants were accepted as part of the overall positive assessment of the optix work. Reviewer 1's comment about optix being 'highly context dependent' directly references these varied regional effects, indicating acceptance of the observations.

result: Lamina structural color can produce nearly all spectral colors (yellow, green, blue, indigo, UV) and even achromatic colors through thickness gradients, as demonstrated by unpigmented scales in several species and rainbow gradient laminae in J. atlites.
evaluation: This was accepted as part of the comprehensive comparative analysis praised by reviewers. Reviewer 2 noted the 'impressive body of comparative data' and Reviewer 3 stated the study was conducted on 'a very broad and sensible selection of specimens,' implicitly accepting these observations across species.

result: Pigment-lamina interactions vary across species and morphs: in J. hierta, yellow pigment and lamina color are mutually reinforcing; in P. octavia, seasonal morphs differ primarily in red pigment concentration rather than lamina thickness, with the wet season morph combining red pigment and blue lamina to produce lightly saturated red.
evaluation: These detailed comparative observations were accepted as part of the overall positive assessment of the comparative work. Reviewer 2 specifically appreciated 'the emphasis on the interaction between structural and pigment colours,' which directly encompasses these findings about how pigments and structural colors combine.
